newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Solvay raises stake in Bulgaria's Sodi to 66.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Solvay raises stake in Bulgaria's Sodi to 66.7 pct.

text.p: Belgian chemicals and drugs group Solvay SA raised its stake to 66.7 percent from 60 percent in Bulgaria's biggest soda ash producer Sodi, company officials said on Friday.

"The increase of Solvay's participation in Sodi will boost confidence of our foreign partners -- suppliers and potential creditors," Solvay Executive committee member Jean Christiaens told a news conference.
Sodi's shareholders meeting on Friday decided to raise its share capital to 6.283 billion levs from 5.236 billion levs, after heated debates.
The new issue will be bought out entirely by Solvay at par value of 1,000 levs, said Christiaens.

Under Bulgaria's biggest sell-off this year the Belgian group acquired 60 percent in Sodi for $160 million in April, pledging to invest an additional $67 million in the next five years to increase dense soda ash capacity from 400,000 tonnes a year at present to the plant's full 1.2 million tonne capacity.
Markets for Sodi's current 800,000 tonnes light soda ash capacity are shrinking, said Christiaens.
The shareholders also agreed to rename the company Devnia-based Solvay Sodi AD. Sodi is one of world's largest synthetic soda ash plants and Solvay's eighth calcinated soda plant.
Christiaens said that through the acquisition it would gain access to markets in the Balkans, the Middle East, and Central Asia.
Solvay Sodi signed a 15-year contract for the use of the nearby Varna harbour on the Black Sea, said Solvay's commercial manager Bruno Brianzoli.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development is expected to complete acquisition of 25 percent of Solvay's 60 percent stake in Sodi in the next two weeks, said EBRD representative in Sofia Tim O'Neil.
Solvay agreed to share Sodi's output capacity with Turkish glass and chemicals producer Sise Cam to reduce pressure on the Italian market.
Under the deal Sise Cam will buy 25 percent of Sodi's production and will buy a $30 million stake in the plant.
The EBRD was considering investing $40 million.
The capital increase caused turmoil among smaller shareholders, who said they will appeal against the decision in court.

"The capital raise violates interests of minor shareholders and we will appeal Solvay's decision in court," Valentin Karabashev manager of a local privatisation fund "Golden Lion" told reporters. -- Elisaveta Konstantinova, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
